title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
interviewTips: Ask if array can contain duplicates, negatives, and unsorted values, and whether O(n) time is required or O(n log n) sorting is acceptable.
Trade-off: sorting is simplest with O(1) extra space but O(n log n) time; hash set gives O(n) time with O(n) space and is expected optimal; union-find is O(n) but has higher constants and more code.
Edge-case tip: empty array returns 0, duplicates must be skipped not counted as breaks, and only start counting when n-1 is absent to avoid O(n^2) re-scanning.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Sorting
approaches.intuition: If we sort the numbers, all consecutive values become adjacent. Then a single linear scan can count runs of x, x+1, x+2 while skipping duplicates. This turns the problem into finding the longest run in a sorted array.
approaches.theory: Sorting imposes total order. After sorting, any consecutive sequence appears as a contiguous block with differences of 0 (duplicate) or 1 (next in sequence). A larger gap ends the current sequence. Maintaining current length and global maximum yields the answer. Correctness follows because sorting preserves set membership and adjacency characterizes consecutiveness.

timeComplexity.explanation: Sorting dominates at O(n log n), linear scan is O(n).

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only constant extra variables besides in-place sort stack, ignoring sort implementation overhead.

steps: Gap 4 to 100 resets cur=1, gap 100 to 200 resets cur=1

edgeCases: Negatives and mixed values handled by same logic

approaches.name: Approach 2: Hash Set with Sequence Start Detection
approaches.intuition: A sequence only needs to be counted once from its smallest element. Put all numbers in a hash set for O(1) lookup, then for each n that has no predecessor n-1, expand forward n+1, n+2 until break. This visits each number at most twice.
approaches.theory: Let S be the set of distinct values. Every maximal consecutive block has a unique start s where s-1 not in S. Expanding only from starts partitions work across blocks with no overlap. Each element is checked once as potential start and once inside a forward walk, giving linear time. Hash set gives expected O(1) membership.

timeComplexity.explanation: Building set is O(n), each distinct number is visited at most twice - once as loop element and once in forward expansion - so expected O(n).

spaceComplexity.explanation: Hash set stores up to n distinct numbers.

steps: 100 has no 99, expand to 100 only, len=1
4 has predecessor 3, skip; 200 has no 199, len=1

edgeCases: Duplicates removed by set, e.g., [1,2,2,3] returns 3
Large gaps do not cause extra work due to start check

approaches.name: Approach 3: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)
approaches.intuition: Treat each distinct number as a node and union it with its neighbor n+1 if present. Each connected component then corresponds exactly to a consecutive sequence, and component size is its length. The answer is the largest component size.
approaches.theory: Union-Find maintains partitions under union operations with path compression and union by size. Initially each value is its own set. For each n, union(n, n+1) when both exist merges adjacent values. By transitivity, all values in interval [a,b] with no gaps end in one set of size b-a+1. Taking max size gives longest consecutive length. Complexity is near-linear due to inverse Ackermann function.

timeComplexity.explanation: Each insert, find and union is almost O(1) amortized where alpha is inverse Ackermann, so effectively O(n).

spaceComplexity.explanation: Parent and size maps store one entry per distinct number.

steps: 100 and 200 have no n+1 neighbor, stay size 1

edgeCases: Duplicates must be deduplicated before init to avoid double counting
Long chain with negatives works the same
